Insects.Ant: One of the most successful insect groups, with colonies in almost every land habitat. Ants can carry objects many times their body weight.
Insects.Bee: Honeybees communicate by waggle dance, which tells hive-mates the direction and distance of flowers.
Insects.Beetle: Beetles make up about a quarter of all known animal species. Their hard front wings fold over the flight wings like a case.
Insects.Butterfly: Butterflies taste with their feet. Their wings are covered in tiny overlapping scales, which give them colour.
Insects.Moth: Moths outnumber butterflies many times over. Some adult moths have no mouth and cannot eat at all.
Insects.Grasshopper: Grasshoppers hear through ears on their abdomens. Many can leap about twenty times their own body length.
Insects.Dragonfly: Dragonflies are expert fliers and have existed since before the dinosaurs. They can catch prey in mid-air with a very high success rate.
Insects.Ladybug: A beetle, not a bug, whose bright spots warn predators it tastes bad. Ladybugs are loved by gardeners for eating aphids.
Insects.Termite: Termites are social insects that build huge mounds. Despite the nickname white ants, they are more closely related to cockroaches.
Insects.Cockroach: Cockroaches have been around for over 300 million years, and they can live for about a week without their heads.
Insects.Mosquito: Only female mosquitoes bite, because they need blood protein for eggs. Mosquitoes are often called the deadliest animal to humans.
Insects.Flea: Fleas can jump over a hundred times their body length. They are insects with flattened bodies, perfect for sliding through fur.
Insects.Firefly: A beetle that lights up through a chemical reaction that produces almost no heat. The glow is used to find mates.
Insects.Spider: A trap: spiders have eight legs and two body parts. Insects have six legs and three body parts, so spiders are arachnids.
Insects.Scorpion: Eight legs and pincers make it an arachnid. Some scorpions glow under ultraviolet light.
Insects.Tick: A tick is an arachnid with eight legs as an adult. It feeds on blood and can spread diseases like Lyme.
Insects.Centipede: Not an insect but a myriapod, with a pair of legs per segment. Its first pair of legs are venomous fangs.
Insects.Millipede: A myriapod with two pairs of legs per segment. Millipedes don't bite and curl up when threatened.
Insects.Woodlouse: A crustacean, closer to a crab than to an insect. It's one of very few crustaceans fully adapted to life on land.
Insects.Earthworm: A segmented worm, not an insect. Earthworms have no legs, and they have five pairs of heart-like vessels.
Insects.Snail: A mollusc with a single coiled shell, not an insect. Snails move on a muscular foot and a layer of slime.
Insects.Crab: A crustacean with ten legs. Crabs have exoskeletons like insects, but they are not insects.
Insects.Mite: A tiny arachnid, not an insect. Adults have eight legs, and some mites live on human faces.
Insects.Slug: A shell-less mollusc, not an insect. Slugs produce slime that helps them glide and protects them from drying out.

Members of the cat family.Lion: Lions are the only cats that live in social groups, and a pride's females do most of the hunting together.
Members of the cat family.Tiger: The largest living cat, a tiger can weigh over 250 kg, and every tiger's stripe pattern is unique.
Members of the cat family.Lynx: Lynx have tufted ears and huge furry paws that work like snowshoes, letting them stalk hares across deep snow.
Members of the cat family.Cheetah: The fastest land animal, a cheetah can hit about 100 km/h, but only in bursts of a few hundred metres.
Members of the cat family.Ocelot: This spotted cat of the Americas was once hunted heavily for its coat, and its pattern looks like chain-link rosettes.
Members of the cat family.Puma: Also called cougar or mountain lion, the puma has more names than any other animal in the Guinness record books.
Members of the cat family.Bobcat: Named for its short, 'bobbed' tail, this North American cat adapts to forests, swamps and even suburbs.
Members of the cat family.Caracal: A caracal can leap about three metres straight up to snatch birds out of the air, helped by its long, black-tufted ears.
Members of the cat family.Serval: With the longest legs relative to body size of any cat, the serval pounces high to catch rodents in tall African grass.
Members of the cat family.Jaguar: The jaguar has the strongest bite of any big cat, strong enough to crack turtle shells and pierce skulls.
Members of the cat family.Snow leopard: Snow leopards can't roar; instead they chuff, and they use their thick tails as scarves in the Himalayan cold.
Members of the cat family.Margay: This small tree-dwelling cat can rotate its ankles 180 degrees, so it descends trunks headfirst like a squirrel.
Members of the cat family.Hyena: Looks dog-like but is not: hyenas form their own family, and are closer to cats and mongooses than to dogs.
Members of the cat family.Civet: Civets are small, cat-like mammals from a separate family; their musk was prized in perfume and some civets help produce a famous coffee.
Members of the cat family.Mongoose: A mongoose can fight a venomous cobra and often win, helped by speed and partial resistance to snake venom.
Members of the cat family.Fossa: This Madagascar predator looks like a cat but is related to mongooses, and it's the island's largest carnivore.
Members of the cat family.Meerkat: Meerkats are mongooses, not cats; they take turns standing guard on hind legs while the rest of the group forages.
Members of the cat family.Wolf: Wolves are canines, the dog family, not cats; they share a lineage with dogs and howl to coordinate the pack.
Members of the cat family.Red panda: Despite the name it's no panda or cat: the red panda belongs to its own family and munches bamboo with a false thumb.
Members of the cat family.Genet: Genets are slim, spotted, cat-like animals but belong to the civet family, and they climb with retractable-style claws.
Members of the cat family.Binturong: The binturong smells like buttered popcorn, and this Southeast Asian relative of civets has a prehensile tail.
Members of the cat family.Wolverine: Wolverines are the largest land weasels, not cats, famed for their ferocity and for crushing frozen bones with their teeth.
Members of the cat family.Raccoon: Raccoons are not cats; they belong to a family of their own, and their sensitive paws help them find food underwater.
Members of the cat family.Coati: Coatis are relatives of raccoons that roam in groups and use their long snouts and flexible noses to root for bugs.

Fungi.Mushroom: Mushrooms are just the fruiting bodies of fungi. The main organism is a hidden web of threads, the mycelium, running through soil or wood.
Fungi.Truffle: Truffles grow underground in partnership with tree roots, and are found by trained pigs or dogs. Prized white ones can sell for thousands of euros per kilo.
Fungi.Yeast: Yeast is a single-celled fungus that makes bread rise and beer ferment. It turns sugar into carbon dioxide and alcohol.
Fungi.Mold: Mold is a fungus that grows as fuzzy threads on damp food. It can spread by releasing countless airborne spores.
Fungi.Toadstool: Toadstool is a folk word for a mushroom, often a poisonous one. There is no botanical difference between a toadstool and a mushroom.
Fungi.Puffball: Puffballs release a cloud of spores when squeezed or stepped on. A giant puffball can reach the size of a football, and produce trillions of spores.
Fungi.Morel: Morels are prized spring mushrooms with honeycomb caps. They must be cooked, since raw ones are toxic, and they're hard to farm.
Fungi.Chanterelle: Chanterelles smell faintly of apricots and are golden and trumpet-shaped. They resist cultivation because they depend on living tree roots.
Fungi.Shiitake: Shiitake grow on hardwood logs and have been cultivated in East Asia for centuries. They're second-most cultivated edible mushroom worldwide.
Fungi.Portobello: The portobello is just a mature cremini, which is a brown button mushroom. It's the same species as the white button mushroom.
Fungi.Penicillium: Penicillium is the mold that gave us penicillin. Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a stray spore had killed bacteria on a dish.
Fungi.Bracket fungus: Bracket fungi grow as shelves on tree trunks and decay wood. Some are tough enough to be used as tinder and were found with Otzi the Iceman.
Fungi.Moss: Moss is a plant, with tiny leaves, though it has no roots and no flowers. It reproduces by spores, like fungi, but is photosynthetic.
Fungi.Algae: Algae photosynthesise like plants, and fungi can't. Some fungi and algae together form lichens, a partnership.
Fungi.Seaweed: Seaweed is a type of algae, not a fungus. Some, like nori for sushi, are important foods.
Fungi.Fern: Ferns are plants that make their own food from sunlight. They reproduce by spores, which is why they get confused with fungi.
Fungi.Bacteria: Bacteria are single-celled organisms in their own kingdom, with no nucleus. There are more bacterial cells in your body than human cells, roughly.
Fungi.Kelp: Kelp is a large brown alga, which forms underwater forests. Giant kelp can grow about half a metre in a day.
Fungi.Plankton: Plankton are drifting organisms, most of them tiny. Phytoplankton produce a large share of the world's oxygen.
Fungi.Sea sponge: Sea sponges are simple animals, not fungi. They have no organs, but can filter huge amounts of water.
Fungi.Coral: Coral is an animal, a colony of tiny polyps. Many get their colour and food from algae living inside them.
Fungi.Liverwort: Liverworts are small, primitive plants. Their name comes from the old belief that they could treat liver disease.
Fungi.Spirulina: Spirulina is a blue-green bacterium, a cyanobacterium, not algae or fungus. It was a food of the Aztecs, and is now a supplement.
Fungi.Sea anemone: Sea anemones are animals related to jellyfish and corals. They sting with tiny harpoon-like cells, though clownfish are immune.

Japanese dishes.Sushi: Sushi began as a way to preserve fish in fermented rice; the rice was originally thrown away, and vinegar later replaced the long fermentation.
Japanese dishes.Ramen: Ramen came from Chinese wheat noodles, and Japan now has instant ramen, a ramen museum in Yokohama, and countless regional styles.
Japanese dishes.Tempura: The frying technique was probably introduced by Portuguese traders in the 1500s, and the light batter is made with ice-cold water.
Japanese dishes.Okonomiyaki: The name means 'grilled as you like it'; Osaka and Hiroshima each claim the definitive version of this savoury pancake.
Japanese dishes.Takoyaki: Octopus balls from Osaka, cooked in a special pan with half-spherical moulds and turned by skewer into crisp, molten-centred spheres.
Japanese dishes.Udon: Thick wheat noodles, often kneaded by foot in traditional shops; Kagawa prefecture is so obsessed that it brands itself the 'Udon Prefecture'.
Japanese dishes.Tonkatsu: A breaded pork cutlet, a Japanese take on European schnitzel from the late 1800s, served with shredded cabbage and a tangy brown sauce.
Japanese dishes.Yakitori: Skewered grilled chicken, where nothing is wasted: menus list everything from thighs to skin, hearts and cartilage.
Japanese dishes.Sashimi: Sliced raw fish served without rice; the quality of the cut and freshness matter most, and the fish is often served with grated daikon.
Japanese dishes.Miso soup: Made from fermented soybean paste in a dashi stock; many Japanese people drink it at breakfast, and the miso is added off the boil to keep its flavour.
Japanese dishes.Onigiri: Rice balls, often wrapped in nori, that have been packed as travel food in Japan for roughly a thousand years.
Japanese dishes.Gyudon: A bowl of rice topped with thinly sliced beef and onions simmered in sweet soy broth, a staple of fast-food chains.
Japanese dishes.Sukiyaki: A hot pot cooked at the table where raw beef and vegetables are dipped in beaten raw egg before eating.
Japanese dishes.Bibimbap: Korean: the name means 'mixed rice', and the dish is served with a fried egg and gochujang, a fermented chili paste.
Japanese dishes.Kimchi: Korea's spicy fermented cabbage; the country is so devoted to it that there are special kimchi refrigerators and a museum.
Japanese dishes.Bulgogi: Korean marinated beef whose name means 'fire meat', so it is grilled, but not Japanese.
Japanese dishes.Pho: Vietnamese beef or chicken noodle soup, often eaten for breakfast, with a broth simmered for many hours with charred ginger and spices.
Japanese dishes.Dim sum: Cantonese small plates served with tea; the tradition is called yum cha, which means 'drink tea'.
Japanese dishes.Pad thai: Thai, not Japanese: rice noodles stir-fried with tamarind, peanuts and lime, a dish promoted as a national symbol in the 1930s and 1940s.
Japanese dishes.Banh mi: A Vietnamese sandwich on a baguette, a legacy of French colonial rule combined with local herbs, pickles and pâté.
Japanese dishes.Laksa: A spicy noodle soup from Malaysia and Singapore, with a coconut-curry or sour tamarind broth; it is not Japanese.
Japanese dishes.Peking duck: Chinese, not Japanese: the duck is roasted until the skin is crisp, then carved at the table and rolled into thin pancakes.
Japanese dishes.Japchae: A Korean dish of glass noodles made from sweet potato starch, stir-fried with vegetables, so it doesn't fit.
Japanese dishes.Kung pao chicken: Chinese, from Sichuan: stir-fried chicken with peanuts and chilies, named for a Qing dynasty official, Ding Baozhen.

Spice blends (not single spices).Garam masala: Garam masala means 'warm spice mix' in Hindi, and every family has its own blend, often with cardamom, cinnamon, cloves and cumin.
Spice blends (not single spices).Za'atar: Za'atar is both a wild thyme-like herb and a Middle Eastern blend of it with sumac and sesame, eaten on flatbread with olive oil.
Spice blends (not single spices).Ras el hanout: Ras el hanout means 'head of the shop' in Arabic, a blend that can contain a dozen or even dozens of spices, chosen by the spice seller.
Spice blends (not single spices).Herbes de Provence: Herbes de Provence is a blend of dried herbs such as thyme, rosemary and savory, and lavender was added mainly for the tourist market.
Spice blends (not single spices).Five-spice: Chinese five-spice usually combines star anise, cloves, Sichuan pepper, cinnamon and fennel, aiming to balance sweet, sour, bitter, pungent and salty.
Spice blends (not single spices).Curry powder: Curry powder is a British-era invention for Indian flavors, rather than a traditional Indian ingredient, as Indian cooks blend spices per dish.
Spice blends (not single spices).Berbere: Berbere is the fiery Ethiopian blend of chilies, fenugreek and many other spices that gives doro wat its deep red color.
Spice blends (not single spices).Old Bay: Old Bay seasoning is a Chesapeake Bay blend of celery salt, paprika and other spices, created in Baltimore in the 1940s for steamed crab.
Spice blends (not single spices).Baharat: Baharat means 'spices' in Arabic, a Middle Eastern blend with black pepper, cumin, cinnamon and others, for meat and rice dishes.
Spice blends (not single spices).Dukkah: Dukkah is an Egyptian mix of crushed nuts, seeds and spices, eaten by dipping bread in olive oil and then into it.
Spice blends (not single spices).Shichimi togarashi: Shichimi togarashi is a Japanese 'seven flavor' blend with chili, sesame, and dried orange peel, sprinkled on noodles and soup.
Spice blends (not single spices).Cajun seasoning: Cajun seasoning is a Louisiana blend, usually paprika, cayenne, garlic and onion, that's less a single recipe than a style.
Spice blends (not single spices).Pumpkin spice: Pumpkin spice contains no pumpkin; it's a mix of cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg and cloves, first used for pumpkin pie.
Spice blends (not single spices).Cumin: Cumin is a single spice, the dried seed of a plant in the parsley family, so it's not a blend.
Spice blends (not single spices).Turmeric: Turmeric is a single spice ground from a root, and curcumin is what colors it deep yellow.
Spice blends (not single spices).Paprika: Paprika is one spice, ground dried peppers, and the smoked Spanish pimentón is a different product.
Spice blends (not single spices).Cinnamon: Cinnamon is a single spice, the dried inner bark of a tree, and the true kind is sweeter and more delicate than the common cassia.
Spice blends (not single spices).Nutmeg: Nutmeg is the seed of a tree, and the lacy red coating around it is another spice, mace.
Spice blends (not single spices).Saffron: Saffron is the dried stigma of a crocus flower, and it takes roughly 150 flowers to produce a single gram, so it's among the priciest spices.
Spice blends (not single spices).Sumac: Sumac is a single spice, dried and ground berries of a shrub, with a lemony tang, and it often goes into za'atar.
Spice blends (not single spices).Cardamom: Cardamom is a single spice, the seed pods of a ginger-family plant, and it's the third most expensive spice by weight.
Spice blends (not single spices).Fenugreek: Fenugreek is a single seed or leaf spice that smells like maple syrup, and it's used in many blends but isn't one.
Spice blends (not single spices).Allspice: Allspice is a single berry, and its name comes from tasting like cinnamon, nutmeg and cloves combined.
Spice blends (not single spices).Asafoetida: Asafoetida is a single spice, a dried resin that smells strongly raw, but turns savory like onion when fried in oil.

Fermented foods and drinks.Kimchi: Kimchi gets its tang from lactic acid bacteria, the same family as in yogurt, and Korea has a museum devoted to it.
Fermented foods and drinks.Sauerkraut: Sauerkraut is just salted cabbage fermented by bacteria, and sailors ate it for vitamin C to prevent scurvy.
Fermented foods and drinks.Yogurt: Yogurt is milk fermented by two bacteria, Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus, which thicken and sour it.
Fermented foods and drinks.Miso: Miso is soybeans fermented with a mold called koji, and darker types are aged longer, sometimes for years.
Fermented foods and drinks.Kombucha: Kombucha is tea fermented with a SCOBY, a symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast, and it contains a tiny bit of alcohol.
Fermented foods and drinks.Beer: Beer is fermented by yeast turning sugars from malted grain into alcohol and CO2, a process at least 7,000 years old.
Fermented foods and drinks.Wine: Wine is fermented grape juice, and yeast living on the grape skins can start the process by itself.
Fermented foods and drinks.Soy sauce: Soy sauce is made by fermenting soybeans and wheat with koji mold and salt, a process that can take months or years.
Fermented foods and drinks.Tempeh: Tempeh is a fermented soybean cake from Indonesia, bound together by a mold, Rhizopus, so it's firm and nutty.
Fermented foods and drinks.Kefir: Kefir is a fermented milk drink made with grains that are actually colonies of yeast and bacteria, tangy and slightly fizzy.
Fermented foods and drinks.Sourdough: Sourdough rises by wild yeast and bacteria rather than commercial yeast, and some starters are kept alive for generations.
Fermented foods and drinks.Natto: Natto is fermented soybeans with a famously sticky, stringy texture, made by Bacillus subtilis bacteria.
Fermented foods and drinks.Vinegar: Vinegar means 'sour wine' in French, made when bacteria turn alcohol into acetic acid, so it's the result of a second fermentation.
Fermented foods and drinks.Tofu: Tofu is made by curdling soy milk with a coagulant, so it's not fermented, unlike its fermented cousin, stinky tofu.
Fermented foods and drinks.Honey: Honey is made by bees from nectar by evaporation and enzymes, not fermentation, and its low water content keeps microbes away.
Fermented foods and drinks.Jam: Jam is preserved by sugar and heat, and no fermentation is involved, though badly stored jam can ferment.
Fermented foods and drinks.Hummus: Hummus is a mashed chickpea and tahini dip, and it isn't fermented, but only blended.
Fermented foods and drinks.Mayonnaise: Mayonnaise is an emulsion of oil, egg and acid, and nothing about it is fermented, but the vinegar in it is.
Fermented foods and drinks.Granola: Granola is baked oats, nuts and sweetener, so it's a baked and not fermented food.
Fermented foods and drinks.Smoked salmon: Smoked salmon is cured with salt and smoke, which preserves it without fermentation.
Fermented foods and drinks.Popcorn: Popcorn is a type of corn whose moisture turns to steam and bursts the hull; no fermentation here.
Fermented foods and drinks.Condensed milk: Condensed milk is milk with water removed and sugar added, so it's preserved by sugar, not fermented.
Fermented foods and drinks.Ghee: Ghee is clarified butter, made by simmering to remove water and milk solids, and it isn't fermented.
Fermented foods and drinks.Raisins: Raisins are grapes dried in the sun, a drying process, not a fermentation.

Landmarks in Italy.Colosseum: Rome's arena had a giant retractable awning, the velarium, which was worked by sailors to shade the crowd.
Landmarks in Italy.Trevi Fountain: Rome's Baroque fountain is where visitors toss coins over a shoulder to ensure a return. Over a million euros a year is collected for charity.
Landmarks in Italy.Pantheon: This 2,000-year-old Roman temple still has the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome, with an open oculus at the top.
Landmarks in Italy.Rialto Bridge: The oldest of four bridges over Venice's Grand Canal was rebuilt in stone in 1591 and is lined with shops.
Landmarks in Italy.St Mark's Basilica: Venice's golden-mosaic church was built to house St Mark's relics, which merchants reputedly smuggled out of Alexandria in 828.
Landmarks in Italy.Mount Vesuvius: The only active volcano on mainland Europe buried Pompeii in AD 79 and still looms over Naples.
Landmarks in Italy.Pompeii: Volcanic ash preserved this Roman town so well that bread, graffiti and street layouts survive nearly 2,000 years on.
Landmarks in Italy.Uffizi: Florence's famed gallery began as Medici offices, since uffizi means offices. It now displays Botticelli's Birth of Venus.
Landmarks in Italy.Ponte Vecchio: Florence's medieval bridge was once lined with butchers' stalls, until the Medici replaced them with goldsmiths.
Landmarks in Italy.Spanish Steps: Rome's grand stairway is named after a nearby Spanish embassy, but it was actually paid for by France.
Landmarks in Italy.Lake Como: This Y-shaped Alpine lake is among Europe's deepest, over 400 m, and its villas have attracted film stars for decades.
Landmarks in Italy.Mount Etna: Sicily's volcano is Europe's tallest active volcano, and it erupts so often that its height changes.
Landmarks in Italy.Acropolis: Athens's hilltop citadel is Greek, not Italian. Its crowning temple, the Parthenon, honors the goddess Athena.
Landmarks in Italy.Sagrada Família: Gaudí's unfinished basilica is in Barcelona, Spain. Construction began in 1882 and has outlasted him by nearly a century.
Landmarks in Italy.Alhambra: This Moorish palace-fortress in Granada, Spain, is famed for intricate stucco, and its name comes from an Arabic word meaning red.
Landmarks in Italy.Parthenon: A trap for Rome lovers. This temple to Athena stands in Athens, Greece, and was once used as a gunpowder store.
Landmarks in Italy.Neuschwanstein: King Ludwig II's Bavarian castle is said to have inspired Disney's Sleeping Beauty Castle, and it is in Germany.
Landmarks in Italy.Charles Bridge: Prague's 14th-century stone bridge is lined with about 30 statues of saints, and it stands in the Czech Republic.
Landmarks in Italy.Hagia Sophia: Built as a cathedral in AD 537 under Justinian, it later became a mosque, then a museum, and a mosque again, in Istanbul.
Landmarks in Italy.Knossos: The Minoan palace on Crete is linked in legend to the labyrinth of the Minotaur, and it belongs to Greece.
Landmarks in Italy.Meteora: Greek monasteries perch on towering sandstone pillars. Monks once hauled supplies up in nets, so it is not an Italian site.
Landmarks in Italy.Plitvice Lakes: Croatia's park has 16 terraced lakes joined by waterfalls, and their turquoise color comes from dissolved minerals.
Landmarks in Italy.Lake Bled: This Slovenian lake has a tiny island with a church, where tradition says couples ring a bell for good luck.
Landmarks in Italy.Dubrovnik Walls: Croatia's medieval city walls stretch nearly 2 km around the old town, and doubled as King's Landing in Game of Thrones.

Things you'll find in Venice.Gondolas: Every gondola is black by a 16th-century law meant to curb showy displays of wealth, and they are built asymmetrically so they steer straight.
Things you'll find in Venice.Rialto Bridge: For centuries it was the only footbridge across the Grand Canal, lined with shops, and it was finished in 1591.
Things you'll find in Venice.St Mark's Square: Napoleon called it the drawing room of Europe, and it floods first when the city's high tides, acqua alta, arrive.
Things you'll find in Venice.Grand Canal: The city's main waterway curves about 3.8 kilometres in an S-shape and is lined with over 170 palaces.
Things you'll find in Venice.Doge's Palace: The seat of Venice's ruler, the doge, and the government's headquarters for centuries, in pink and white Gothic marble.
Things you'll find in Venice.Murano: This island has produced Venice's famous glass since 1291, when furnaces were moved there from the city to reduce fire risk.
Things you'll find in Venice.Burano: A lagoon island with brightly painted houses and a tradition of lace-making.
Things you'll find in Venice.Bridge of Sighs: Linking the Doge's Palace to the prison, it is said to be named for convicts' last view of freedom.
Things you'll find in Venice.Vaporetto: Venice's water bus is the city's public transport, since cars and bikes can't enter its historic centre.
Things you'll find in Venice.Lido: A barrier island that hosts the Venice Film Festival, the oldest in the world, since 1932.
Things you'll find in Venice.Torcello: A nearly deserted island that was once the lagoon's first settled and main centre, before Venice grew.
Things you'll find in Venice.Colosseum: Rome's amphitheatre could hold about 50,000, so it's not in Venice.
Things you'll find in Venice.Trevi Fountain: Rome's baroque fountain, where visitors toss in around a million euros a year, and so isn't here.
Things you'll find in Venice.Uffizi: Florence's art museum, home of Botticelli's Birth of Venus, in a former administrative building.
Things you'll find in Venice.Spanish Steps: Rome's 135-step stair, called Spanish for the nearby embassy, not found in Venice.
Things you'll find in Venice.Ponte Vecchio: Florence's medieval bridge over the Arno, lined with goldsmiths, and the only one the Germans spared in 1944.
Things you'll find in Venice.Pompeii: A Roman city near Naples, buried by Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD.
Things you'll find in Venice.Pantheon: Rome's ancient temple has a concrete dome that remains the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome.
Things you'll find in Venice.Sistine Chapel: In the Vatican, where Michelangelo painted the ceiling between 1508 and 1512, so not in Venice.
Things you'll find in Venice.Boboli Gardens: Florence's grand Renaissance garden behind the Pitti Palace, not in Venice.
Things you'll find in Venice.Leaning Tower: Pisa's famous bell tower started tilting during construction, due to soft soil, and it's far from Venice.
Things you'll find in Venice.Vesuvius: The volcano near Naples, whose 79 AD eruption buried Pompeii, is in the south of Italy.
Things you'll find in Venice.Amalfi Coast: A cliffside stretch of southern Italy famous for lemons, not near Venice.
Things you'll find in Venice.Duomo di Milano: Milan's marble Gothic cathedral took nearly six centuries to complete, and has thousands of statues.

Places in Portugal.Lisbon: One of Europe's oldest capitals, it is older than London and Paris, and was largely rebuilt after the huge 1755 earthquake.
Places in Portugal.Porto: The city that gave port wine its name, and where Harry Potter author J. K. Rowling once taught English.
Places in Portugal.Algarve: Portugal's southern coast is famed for golden cliffs and sea caves, with over 300 days of sunshine per year.
Places in Portugal.Sintra: A fairy-tale hill town of palaces, including the colorful Pena Palace, once a summer retreat for Portuguese royalty.
Places in Portugal.Madeira: This Atlantic island is famous for fortified wine and flower festivals, and is the birthplace of footballer Cristiano Ronaldo.
Places in Portugal.Azores: Nine volcanic islands in the mid-Atlantic, closer to North America than mainland Portugal, known for whale watching.
Places in Portugal.Faro: The gateway to the Algarve, with a charming old town and a lagoon park that attracts flamingos.
Places in Portugal.Coimbra: Home to one of Europe's oldest universities, founded in 1290, with a gilded baroque library full of books and bats.
Places in Portugal.Évora: A walled city with a Roman temple still standing and a chapel decorated entirely with human bones.
Places in Portugal.Cascais: A former fishing village turned seaside resort west of Lisbon, once the favored retreat of European royalty in exile.
Places in Portugal.Douro Valley: The world's oldest demarcated wine region, with terraced vineyards that produce port, laid out in 1756.
Places in Portugal.Braga: One of Portugal's oldest cities and a major religious center, known for its processions at Easter.
Places in Portugal.Seville: This Spanish city in Andalusia is the home of flamenco, and just across the border from Portugal.
Places in Portugal.Vigo: A Galician port city in northwest Spain, just north of the border with Portugal.
Places in Portugal.Bilbao: Spain's Basque city, now known for the titanium-clad Guggenheim Museum designed by Frank Gehry.
Places in Portugal.Málaga: Pablo Picasso's birthplace is on Spain's Costa del Sol, far from Portugal; his birth house is now a museum.
Places in Portugal.Canary Islands: Spanish volcanic islands off the African coast, far southeast of Portugal's Madeira.
Places in Portugal.Ibiza: A Spanish party island in the Balearics that is also a World Heritage Site for its old town and seagrass meadows.
Places in Portugal.Andorra: A tiny Pyrenees principality between Spain and France, with no airport and two co-princes, one of them the French president.
Places in Portugal.Cape Verde: An island nation off West Africa that was once a Portuguese colony, but is independent and not part of Portugal today.
Places in Portugal.Galicia: Spanish region in the northwest, bordering Portugal, with a Celtic heritage and bagpipes, and the Camino de Santiago's end.
Places in Portugal.Tangier: Across the Strait of Gibraltar in Morocco, not in Portugal, though Portugal once held it from 1471 to 1661.
Places in Portugal.Cádiz: A Spanish city on the Atlantic, claimed to be one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in western Europe.
Places in Portugal.Majorca: The largest of Spain's Balearic Islands, in the Mediterranean, nowhere near Portugal.

Scottish islands.Skye: The largest of the Inner Hebrides, dominated by the jagged Cuillin mountains and linked to the mainland by a bridge since 1995.

Things found in your blood.Red blood cells: They make up about 40 percent of blood by volume. Mature ones have no nucleus, which makes room for more hemoglobin, and each lives about four months.
Things found in your blood.White blood cells: Your immune soldiers. They are far fewer than red cells, and a count of them is one of the first things a doctor checks for infection.
Things found in your blood.Platelets: Tiny cell fragments that clump to plug cuts. They live only about a week to ten days, so your body makes new ones constantly.
Things found in your blood.Plasma: The pale yellow liquid that makes up over half of blood. It's mostly water, and it can be donated separately from blood.
Things found in your blood.Hemoglobin: The iron-rich protein that carries oxygen and makes blood red. Each red cell holds hundreds of millions of copies.
Things found in your blood.Glucose: Blood sugar, your cells' main fuel. Insulin keeps it in a narrow range, and diabetes is a failure of that control.
Things found in your blood.Antibodies: Y-shaped proteins that lock onto germs. After an infection or vaccine, some stay in your blood for years as a defense.
Things found in your blood.Oxygen: Carried through the blood mostly by hemoglobin. Blood leaving the lungs is bright red since it is loaded with it.
Things found in your blood.Hormones: Chemical messengers like insulin and adrenaline travel through the blood to distant organs. Tiny amounts can cause big effects.
Things found in your blood.Water: Blood is roughly half water, and plasma is about 90 percent water. Dehydration makes it thicker.
Things found in your blood.Cholesterol: A waxy fat your liver makes and your body needs for cell walls. It travels in blood inside carriers called LDL and HDL.
Things found in your blood.Dentin: A trap: this is the hard layer under tooth enamel. It's part of the tooth, not found in blood.
Things found in your blood.Saliva: Made by glands in your mouth, not in blood. You produce around a liter or more a day.
Things found in your blood.Enamel: The hardest substance in the human body, and covering your teeth. It contains no living cells and isn't in blood.
Things found in your blood.Keratin: The tough protein in hair, nails and the top layer of skin. It's a structural protein, not something floating in blood.
Things found in your blood.Cartilage: The flexible tissue in your nose, ears and joints. It has no blood supply of its own, which is why it heals slowly.
Things found in your blood.Mucus: Slimy stuff that coats and protects your nose, throat and gut. You swallow most of what you make each day.
Things found in your blood.Stomach acid: Hydrochloric acid in your stomach, strong enough to dissolve metal. It stays in the stomach, not the blood.
Things found in your blood.Neurons: Nerve cells in your brain and nerves, not blood. Your brain has about 86 billion of them.
Things found in your blood.Bone marrow: The soft tissue inside bones where blood cells are made. It makes blood, but isn't in it.
Things found in your blood.Tears: Made by glands near the eye, and not part of blood. Emotional tears contain stress hormones, unlike those from onion fumes.
Things found in your blood.Hair: Hair is dead keratin, other than the root. It grows about half an inch a month, and isn't carried in blood.
Things found in your blood.Sweat: Made by glands in your skin, mostly water and a little salt. It cools you as it evaporates.
Things found in your blood.Earwax: Produced by glands in your ear canal. It traps dust and germs, and comes in wet or dry forms depending on your genes.

Symbols used in sheet music.Treble clef: The treble clef is a stylized letter G that curls around the second line of the staff, marking where G above middle C sits.
Symbols used in sheet music.Bass clef: The bass clef derives from a stylized letter F, with its two dots surrounding the line that is F below middle C.
Symbols used in sheet music.Sharp: A sharp raises a note by a half step, and the symbol evolved from a medieval form of the letter b.
Symbols used in sheet music.Flat: A flat lowers a note by a half step, and its shape comes from a rounded lowercase 'b'.
Symbols used in sheet music.Natural: A natural cancels a previous sharp or flat, restoring the plain note for the rest of the measure.
Symbols used in sheet music.Fermata: A fermata, often called the bird's eye, tells a performer to hold a note longer than written, at their own discretion.
Symbols used in sheet music.Rest: Every note value has a matching rest, so silence in music is written as carefully as sound.
Symbols used in sheet music.Time signature: The two stacked numbers say how many beats are in each measure and which note value gets the beat.
Symbols used in sheet music.Repeat sign: Repeat signs are two dots beside thick bars, telling players to go back and play a passage again.
Symbols used in sheet music.Slur: A slur is a curved line over notes that tells a performer to play them smoothly, with no break between.
Symbols used in sheet music.Hashtag: Trap: the hashtag looks like a sharp sign, but the musical sharp has two slanted bars, not tilted ones.
Symbols used in sheet music.Ampersand: Trap: the ampersand is a typographic ligature of 'et', Latin for 'and', and not a music symbol.
Symbols used in sheet music.Asterisk: Trap: the asterisk means a footnote in text and has no standard role in notation.
Symbols used in sheet music.Percent sign: Trap: the percent sign is arithmetic, but repeated bars are shown with a similar slash-and-dots sign.
Symbols used in sheet music.Pi: Trap: pi is a math constant of about 3.14159, not a musical notation sign.
Symbols used in sheet music.Infinity sign: Trap: the infinity sign belongs to math, not to scores.
Symbols used in sheet music.Peace sign: Trap: the peace sign was made in 1958 for nuclear disarmament, not for music.
Symbols used in sheet music.Copyright sign: Trap: it can appear at the bottom of a score, but it is not a notation symbol that tells you how to play.
Symbols used in sheet music.At sign: Trap: the at sign is used in email, not in music.
Symbols used in sheet music.Euro sign: Trap: the euro sign stands for a currency, not a note.
Symbols used in sheet music.Plus sign: Trap: it can mean a stopped note for some brass players, though it is not among the main symbols.
Symbols used in sheet music.Checkmark: Trap: a checkmark is not a standard music symbol, though teachers use it to mark homework.
Symbols used in sheet music.Degree sign: Trap: the degree sign is used for temperature, but chord charts use a small circle for diminished chords.
Symbols used in sheet music.Paragraph mark: Trap: the pilcrow marks text paragraphs and has no place in a score.
