Rock climbing gear.Carabiner: The word comes from the German for spring hook, and a locking gate keeps a loaded carabiner from opening in a fall.
Rock climbing gear.Harness: Waist and leg loops spread a fall's force over the body, and the climber ties the rope directly into it.
Rock climbing gear.Belay device: This device creates friction on the rope so a belayer can catch a falling climber or lower them safely.
Rock climbing gear.Chalk bag: Magnesium carbonate dust absorbs sweat from the hands, so climbers can keep a firm grip on tiny holds.
Rock climbing gear.Climbing shoes: They are worn tight, often a size or more smaller than street shoes, with sticky rubber that grips rock.
Rock climbing gear.Quickdraw: Two carabiners joined by a short sewn sling let the rope run smoothly through bolts as a climber rises.
Rock climbing gear.Rope: Dynamic ropes stretch to absorb the shock of a fall, unlike static ropes used for hauling gear.
Rock climbing gear.Helmet: It guards against falling rocks and knocks to the head, which is now standard in most outdoor climbing.
Rock climbing gear.Crash pad: Thick foam pads cushion falls in bouldering, where climbers tackle short problems without ropes.
Rock climbing gear.Cam: Ray Jardine's spring-loaded camming devices, called Friends in the late 1970s, grip cracks in rock as they expand.
Rock climbing gear.Bobber: An angler's float bobs when a fish bites, but it has no place on a rock face.
Rock climbing gear.Sinker: A fishing sinker is a weight, often lead, that pulls the bait down; climbers carry nothing like it.
Rock climbing gear.Lure: A lure is fishing bait made to look like prey, so it's no climbing gear, though both sports need patience.
Rock climbing gear.Saddle: A saddle is horse tack, but also a low point between two peaks on a ridge, a trap for climbers.
Rock climbing gear.Paddle: A paddle drives canoes and kayaks, which means it belongs on the water, not on rock.
Rock climbing gear.Snorkel: A snorkel lets swimmers breathe face-down at the surface, which a climber has no use for.
Rock climbing gear.Flippers: Flippers help swimmers and divers push water, but they would make climbing very awkward.
Rock climbing gear.Skateboard: A skateboard rolls on pavement, and wheels are no help on a vertical rock wall.
Rock climbing gear.Shuttlecock: A shuttlecock is badminton's feathered projectile, which reaches more than 200 mph off a smash; not climbing gear.
Rock climbing gear.Tackle box: An angler's tackle box holds hooks, lures and line, while climbers keep their gear on a harness gear loop.
Rock climbing gear.Easel: An easel holds a painter's canvas upright, and climbers hang from their ropes instead.
Rock climbing gear.Kiln: A kiln fires clay at very high heat for potters, and it has no place on a cliff.
Rock climbing gear.Oar: An oar is rowing gear, and gripping one would not help you grip a cliff.
Rock climbing gear.Hockey stick: A hockey stick belongs on ice, while an ice climber carries a pair of axes for slippery slopes.

Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.E: The most common English letter, and the one that appears in the most five-letter words. It is worth just 1 point despite showing up 12 times in the tiles.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.A: With nine copies, A is tied for second most common tile. Alfred Butts based tile values on letter counts from the New York Times.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.I: Nine I tiles are in the set, and it's the vowel most likely to be stuck with duplicates, since many words use just one.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.O: There are eight O tiles. Vowels dominate the 1-point group, which is why racks without them are so hard to play.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.N: N has six tiles and often anchors words with -ING or -ION endings, so it's a dependable 1-point letter.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.R: R has six tiles and helps form prefixes like RE-. It's one of the letters in RSTLNE, the strong bingo letters.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.T: T has six tiles and sits at the end of many words. It pairs with E, R, S to make the best bingo racks.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.L: L has four tiles. It is one of the more flexible consonants, forming blends like BL, CL, and PL.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.S: Only four S tiles, yet it is prized: adding an S to a word can open a lane for a 50-point bingo, so skilled players hoard it.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.U: Four U tiles, and the clumsiest vowel: it is the one most players want to dump, especially if the Q is still on the rack.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.Q: Q is the 10-point letter, with just one tile. Words like QI, QAT, and QADI let you play it without a U.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.Z: Z is worth 10 points. ZA, ZEN, and ZOO are common ways to cash it in, and there is only one in the bag.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.J: J is worth 8 points, with only one tile. JO and JA are accepted short plays, which makes J easier than it looks.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.X: X is worth 8 points, and 'XI', 'XU', and 'AX' let it sit on double-letter squares for strong two-way plays.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.K: Worth 5 points with only one tile in the bag. It sits alone in the mid-value tier, between the 4-pointers and the 8-pointers.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.F: F is worth 4 points, same as H, V, W, and Y. Two tiles are in the bag.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.H: H is worth 4 points. Two H tiles exist, and it helps form common digraphs like SH, TH, and CH.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.V: Worth 4 points, but short V words are scarce: there are no two-letter ones in the standard dictionary, which makes it awkward to dump.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.W: W is worth 4 points and has two tiles. Its value is a bit higher than you'd expect, given how many common words contain it.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.Y: Y is worth 4 points. It can behave like a vowel, which makes its two tiles pretty flexible for building words.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.B: B is worth 3 points, two tiles in the bag. The 3-point group also includes C, M, and P.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.C: Worth 3 points with two tiles. It is a surprisingly weak tile in Scrabble: no two-letter word uses C at all.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.M: M is worth 3 points. It has two tiles and works well in short plays like MA, MI, and OM.
Letters worth 1 point in Scrabble.P: P is worth 3 points, with two tiles. It sits with B, C, and M in the middle tier of tile values.

Sports that don't use a ball.Curling: Granite stones weighing about 20 kg glide on pebbled ice while sweepers polish the path, and it's often called chess on ice.
Sports that don't use a ball.Fencing: A hit is registered electrically, and the blades are wired so that touches are detected by sensors.
Sports that don't use a ball.Archery: Olympic archers shoot at a target 70 meters away, and the bullseye is about the size of a CD.
Sports that don't use a ball.Rowing: Rowers face backward and see where they've been, and crews of eight are steered by a coxswain.
Sports that don't use a ball.Boxing: Fighters went bare-knuckle until padded gloves became standard in the late 1800s under the Queensberry rules.
Sports that don't use a ball.Swimming: The Olympic freestyle is the fastest stroke, and a pool is 50 meters long for the Games.
Sports that don't use a ball.Ice hockey: A hard rubber puck, frozen before games to cut bouncing, stands in for a ball.
Sports that don't use a ball.Badminton: It's played with a feathered shuttlecock, and it's named after Badminton House in England.
Sports that don't use a ball.Luge: Riders lie feet-first on a sled and can reach over 140 km/h, and they steer with their calves and shoulders.
Sports that don't use a ball.Judo: Created in 1882 by Jigoro Kano, its name means gentle way, and it became an Olympic sport in 1964.
Sports that don't use a ball.Darts: Players throw darts at a board, and a perfect game, a nine-darter, takes just nine throws.
Sports that don't use a ball.Cycling: A bicycle replaces the ball, and the Tour de France takes about three weeks, covering around 3,500 km.
Sports that don't use a ball.Netball: It's a ball game with hoops and no dribbling, and it was derived from early basketball.
Sports that don't use a ball.Handball: Players throw a ball into goals, with a ball of course.
Sports that don't use a ball.Squash: Players hit a small rubber ball against walls with racquets, so a ball is needed.
Sports that don't use a ball.Croquet: Mallets hit balls through hoops, so it's a ball sport.
Sports that don't use a ball.Polo: Mounted players hit a ball with mallets, so it's a ball sport.
Sports that don't use a ball.Bowling: A heavy ball is rolled at pins, and a perfect game is 12 strikes, a score of 300.
Sports that don't use a ball.Water polo: Swimmers throw a ball into goals, with a ball needed, and it began in 19th-century England as rugby in water.
Sports that don't use a ball.Lacrosse: A small rubber ball is thrown in a netted stick, and it's a ball game.
Sports that don't use a ball.Cricket: A hard leather ball is bowled to batters, and the game needs a ball.
Sports that don't use a ball.Golf: The sport is about hitting a ball into a hole, and the ball has dimples to fly further.
Sports that don't use a ball.Billiards: Cue sports use balls, and the name goes back to the 15th century.
Sports that don't use a ball.Bocce: Players throw balls toward a smaller target ball, the pallino, and it's an Italian game that needs balls.

Fencing terms.Foil: A light thrusting weapon where only hits to the torso score, and the right-of-way rules decide who gets the point.
Fencing terms.Epee: The heaviest of the three weapons, with the whole body as a target, and there is no right of way.
Fencing terms.Sabre: Fencing's cut-and-thrust weapon, descended from cavalry swords, scoring above the waist, and the fastest of the three.
Fencing terms.Lunge: The basic attacking move, where the front leg extends rapidly while the back leg pushes, striking from a distance.
Fencing terms.Parry: A defensive block of the opponent's blade, which gives the defender a chance to riposte.
Fencing terms.Riposte: A counterattack made right after a parry, and the word comes from the Italian for 'reply'.
Fencing terms.En garde: The command to take the ready position, from the French 'on guard', before the bout begins.
Fencing terms.Touche: A French word for 'touched', which a fencer says to acknowledge a hit.
Fencing terms.Piste: The strip, 14 metres long, on which fencing takes place, and its end lines warn fencers they're out of space.
Fencing terms.Lame: A metallic jacket worn in foil and sabre, which lets the scoring machine register valid target hits, and it is pronounced 'lah-may'.
Fencing terms.Fleche: A running attack, from the French for 'arrow', which is common in foil and epee.
Fencing terms.Allez: The referee's cry meaning 'go' when a bout restarts, from French.
Fencing terms.Bout: A fencing match, which in competition ends at 15 touches for the direct elimination rounds, or at time.
Fencing terms.Jab: A quick straight punch in boxing, and not a fencing term.
Fencing terms.Uppercut: A boxing punch that comes upward from below, so it belongs in the ring, not on the piste.
Fencing terms.Volley: A tennis shot hit before the ball bounces, and no part of fencing.
Fencing terms.Lob: A high arcing shot in tennis, not fencing.
Fencing terms.Slam dunk: A basketball score, thrust down through the hoop.
Fencing terms.Ollie: A skateboarding trick named after Alan 'Ollie' Gelfand, in which the board pops up with the rider.
Fencing terms.Birdie: A golf score of one under par, whose name comes from early-1900s American slang for something excellent.
Fencing terms.Wicket: A cricket term for the three stumps and two bails, and also for a dismissal.
Fencing terms.Checkmate: A chess term, from the Persian for 'the king is helpless', not fencing.
Fencing terms.Scrum: A rugby restart in which the packs push against each other, so no swords.
Fencing terms.Bunt: A baseball tap with a bat, where the hitter does not swing.

Sporting events held every four years.Summer Olympics: The modern Games began in Athens in 1896. They run on a four-year cycle called an Olympiad, though 2020 was postponed to 2021.
Sporting events held every four years.Winter Olympics: First held in Chamonix, France, in 1924. They ran in the same year as the Summer Games until 1994, when they shifted two years apart.
Sporting events held every four years.FIFA World Cup: The men's tournament began in 1930 in Uruguay. It's one of the most-watched events on Earth and is held every four years.
Sporting events held every four years.Commonwealth Games: A multi-sport event for nations once under British rule, first held in 1930 as the British Empire Games. It takes place every four years.
Sporting events held every four years.Rugby World Cup: First held in 1987 in New Zealand and Australia. The winners receive the Webb Ellis Cup, named after the legendary inventor of the game.
Sporting events held every four years.UEFA Euros: Europe's national-team football championship, first played in 1960. It falls in the middle of the World Cup's four-year cycle.
Sporting events held every four years.Asian Games: Held every four years since 1951, the first being in New Delhi. It is the second-largest multi-sport event after the Olympics.
Sporting events held every four years.Pan American Games: A multi-sport event for nations of the Americas, first held in 1951 in Buenos Aires. It is held every four years in the year before the Olympics.
Sporting events held every four years.Cricket World Cup: The one-day tournament began in 1975 in England. It gets enormous audiences in South Asia, and it now happens every four years.
Sporting events held every four years.Paralympics: Growing from a 1948 contest for wounded soldiers at Stoke Mandeville, England. The Games now run every four years after each Olympics.
Sporting events held every four years.Women's World Cup: First played in 1991 in China. It has run every four years since, and the 2023 edition expanded to 32 teams.
Sporting events held every four years.Ryder Cup: A golf contest between the US and Europe. It's held every two years, and it's famous for fierce crowds and team spirit.
Sporting events held every four years.Super Bowl: The American football finale, held annually since 1967. It is a yearly event, and it draws one of the biggest TV audiences in the US.
Sporting events held every four years.Wimbledon: The oldest tennis tournament, first played in 1877. It happens every year, with strict all-white dress rules for players.
Sporting events held every four years.Tour de France: The famed cycling race, first held in 1903. It happens annually in July and covers about 3,500 kilometers.
Sporting events held every four years.Kentucky Derby: The first jewel of the Triple Crown, run since 1875. It is held annually, on the first Saturday in May, at Churchill Downs.
Sporting events held every four years.Stanley Cup Final: The championship series of the NHL, held every year. The Cup itself dates to 1892 and is the oldest trophy in pro sports in North America.
Sporting events held every four years.The Masters: A golf major played every April at Augusta National. The winner receives a green jacket, which is an annual tradition.
Sporting events held every four years.World Series: Baseball's championship, played every October since 1903. It is annual, though 1994 was lost to a strike.
Sporting events held every four years.Davis Cup: The men's team tennis competition begun in 1900. It is annual and now ends with a finals week.
Sporting events held every four years.Solheim Cup: A women's golf contest between the US and Europe. It is held every two years and mirrors the Ryder Cup.
Sporting events held every four years.NBA Finals: The basketball championship, played each June. It is a yearly series, and the winner earns the Larry O'Brien Trophy.
Sporting events held every four years.Boston Marathon: The oldest annual marathon, held since 1897. It takes place on Patriots' Day each April and requires qualifying times.
Sporting events held every four years.Grand National: The famously demanding steeplechase run at Aintree near Liverpool. It is annual, with big fences like Becher's Brook.

Sun gods and goddesses.Ra: The Egyptian sun god, who was thought to sail across the sky by day and through the underworld at night in a boat.
Sun gods and goddesses.Helios: The Greek sun god who drove a fiery chariot across the sky daily. The Colossus of Rhodes honored him.
Sun gods and goddesses.Sol: The Roman sun god, whose name gave us "solar." Emperor Aurelian made him the state's chief god in 274 AD.
Sun gods and goddesses.Amaterasu: Japan's sun goddess, who hid in a cave and plunged the world into darkness. The imperial family claims descent from her.
Sun gods and goddesses.Inti: The Incan sun god, and the Inca emperor was believed to be his son. The Sol and Inti were also names of Peruvian currency.
Sun gods and goddesses.Surya: The Hindu sun god, who rides a chariot pulled by seven horses. He is honored daily with greetings and yoga.
Sun gods and goddesses.Tonatiuh: The Aztec sun god, who needed human sacrifice to keep the sun moving. He is at the center of the Aztec calendar stone.
Sun gods and goddesses.Aten: The sun disk that the pharaoh Akhenaten raised above all other gods. This was a short-lived attempt at one-god worship.
Sun gods and goddesses.Shamash: The Mesopotamian sun god of justice, shown handing laws to Hammurabi on his famous stele.
Sun gods and goddesses.Selene: A trap: the Greek moon goddess, not a sun deity. She drove a moon chariot across the night sky.
Sun gods and goddesses.Luna: The Roman moon goddess. The word gives us "lunar" and "lunatic."
Sun gods and goddesses.Thoth: The Egyptian god of writing and wisdom, linked with the moon, and is shown as an ibis or baboon. The moon is his, not the sun.
Sun gods and goddesses.Khonsu: The Egyptian moon god, his name meaning "traveler." He was seen crossing the night sky.
Sun gods and goddesses.Artemis: Greek goddess of the hunt and the moon, twin of Apollo. Later tradition made her the moon where Apollo was the sun.
Sun gods and goddesses.Thor: The Norse thunder god, whose hammer Mjolnir is his emblem. He rules storms and strength, not the sun.
Sun gods and goddesses.Poseidon: Greek god of the sea, with no solar role.
Sun gods and goddesses.Hades: Greek lord of the underworld, the opposite of the bright sun.
Sun gods and goddesses.Odin: The Norse chief god of wisdom and war, who sacrificed an eye for knowledge. Not a sun god.
Sun gods and goddesses.Hera: Greek queen of the gods and goddess of marriage, no connection to the sun.
Sun gods and goddesses.Ares: The Greek war god, disliked even by his father Zeus. He had no solar role, as the sun belonged to Helios.
Sun gods and goddesses.Isis: The Egyptian goddess of magic and motherhood. She's often shown with a sun disk between horns, but she's not the sun god.
Sun gods and goddesses.Mani: A Norse moon god who drives the moon across the sky, chased by wolves. He is the moon, not the sun.
Sun gods and goddesses.Diana: The Roman goddess of the hunt, associated with the moon, so not the sun.
Sun gods and goddesses.Tsukuyomi: Japanese moon god, brother of the sun goddess Amaterasu. Their separation is why day and night never meet.

Celtic myth and folklore.Cuchulainn: Ulster's hero, whose battle fury warped his body; he died tied to a standing stone so he could face enemies upright.
Celtic myth and folklore.Fionn mac Cumhaill: The Irish giant-hero gained wisdom by tasting the Salmon of Knowledge; his thumb gave him insight.
Celtic myth and folklore.Brigid: An Irish goddess of poetry, healing and smithcraft, later folded into St. Brigid, whose feast Imbolc marks the start of spring.
Celtic myth and folklore.Morrigan: An Irish battle goddess who appears as a crow, and is said to have foretold Cuchulainn's death.
Celtic myth and folklore.Lugh: A multi-skilled Irish god, whose name is the source of the city name Lyon, and who is celebrated on the festival of Lughnasadh in August.
Celtic myth and folklore.Dagda: The 'good god' of Ireland's Tuatha De Danann, who owned a cauldron that never ran dry and a club that could kill and revive.
Celtic myth and folklore.Banshee: In Irish folklore, her wail outside a house is said to foretell a death in the family.
Celtic myth and folklore.Leprechaun: The Irish shoemaker fairy who guards a pot of gold; if captured, he must give up three wishes or his treasure.
Celtic myth and folklore.Selkie: Seals who shed their skin to become human; a person who hides the skin could force the selkie to stay.
Celtic myth and folklore.Tir na nOg: The Land of the Young in Irish myth, where no one ages; Oisin returned to Ireland after what he thought was three years, and aged to dust.
Celtic myth and folklore.Oisin: Fionn's poet son, who lived in Tir na nOg for what seemed three years but was three centuries back home.
Celtic myth and folklore.Danu: Mother goddess of the Tuatha De Danann ('people of Danu'), and the Danube is possibly named for her.
Celtic myth and folklore.Odin: A trap: the one-eyed Norse chief god, who traded an eye for wisdom, is Germanic and not Celtic.
Celtic myth and folklore.Thor: A trap: the Norse thunder god is not Celtic; Celtic thunder belonged to gods like Taranis.
Celtic myth and folklore.Zeus: A trap: the Greek king of the gods is not Celtic; Celtic sky gods such as Taranis ('thunder') had that role.
Celtic myth and folklore.Ra: A trap: the Egyptian sun god belongs to another tradition; the Celtic sun god is often linked with Belenus.
Celtic myth and folklore.Fenrir: A trap: the monstrous wolf is Norse, bound by the gods and fated to devour Odin at Ragnarok.
Celtic myth and folklore.Valkyrie: Norse battle maidens, not Celtic, though the Morrigan plays a similar role in Irish tales.
Celtic myth and folklore.Medusa: A trap: the snake-haired Gorgon is Greek, and could turn onlookers to stone.
Celtic myth and folklore.Anubis: A trap: the jackal-headed god of embalming is Egyptian, not Celtic.
Celtic myth and folklore.Loki: A trap: this Norse trickster god is a shape-shifter, and part of Scandinavian rather than Celtic myth.
Celtic myth and folklore.Freya: A trap: Norse goddess of love and war, whose chariot is drawn by cats; Celtic myth has Brigid.
Celtic myth and folklore.Hercules: A trap: the Roman name for Greek Heracles, strongman of the Twelve Labors, with no Celtic link.
Celtic myth and folklore.Golem: A trap: a clay figure from Jewish folklore, said to be made by rabbis, not Celtic.

Gear a Roman legionary carried.Gladius: The short sword of the legions, about 50 to 60 cm, built for stabbing in tight formation. The word is Latin for sword and gives us "gladiator".
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Pilum: A heavy javelin whose soft iron neck bent on impact, so the enemy couldn't throw it back, and it also dragged down their shield.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Shield: The curved rectangular scutum, made of glued wooden planks and covered with leather. In the testudo ("tortoise") formation, shields overlapped front and top.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Dagger: The pugio, a short blade carried on the belt as a backup. Roman soldiers took pride in decorating theirs with silver inlay.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Helmet: A metal galea with neck guard and cheek plates. Its design changed over time, and the Imperial Gallic types had ridges against sword blows.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Woolen cloak: The sagum, a heavy rectangular wool cloak, was pinned at the shoulder. It was a soldier's blanket as well as protection against rain and cold.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Hobnailed sandals: Caligae had iron studs in the sole, which clattered on stone roads. Emperor Caligula got his nickname, "little boots", from a child-size pair.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Pickaxe: Legionaries were also builders, carrying a dolabra, which was part pick and part axe. A marching army could dig a fortified camp every night.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Cooking pot: Each section of eight men shared a pot and mule, and soldiers carried their own mess kit. Rations were mainly wheat and sour wine.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Chainmail: The lorica hamata, mail of thousands of tiny rings, weighed around 11 kg. It was probably adopted from the Celts, who invented it.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Musket: Black-powder muskets appeared about 1,300 years after Rome's western empire fell. Roman troops relied on swords, spears and artillery.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Rifle: Rifles with spiral grooves were developed centuries later. No Roman had one.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Katana: A Japanese sword, forged in a land far from Rome and used from the medieval age. The legions carried a short gladius.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Bayonet: It was invented in 17th-century France, reportedly in Bayonne. Romans simply used spears with sharp heads.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Grenade: Explosive grenades needed gunpowder, unknown in Rome. The Byzantines had fire weapons, but the legion did not.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Revolver: The revolver came in the 1830s with Samuel Colt, nearly 2,000 years after Rome's heyday.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Chainsaw: Created for medical use, in childbirth, in the late 1800s. A Roman soldier would have gaped at a petrol-powered saw.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Flashlight: Needs batteries, which weren't invented until 1800. The Romans used torches and oil lamps.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Smartphone: An evident intruder. The Romans had signal flags and fire beacons along the frontier, and wrote on wax tablets.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Tomahawk: A Native American axe, used in a continent the Romans never knew. Roman axes were for building and fighting.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Boomerang: An Aboriginal Australian hunting tool. Returning boomerangs were made in Australia thousands of years ago, an unreachable distance for Rome.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Nunchucks: Associated with East Asia and martial arts, not with Rome. Their exact origins are debated.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Top hat: A 19th-century fashion. A Roman soldier wore a helmet, and a civilian wore a toga.
Gear a Roman legionary carried.Wristwatch: Wristwatches came into use around 1900. The Romans told time by sundials and water clocks.

Things at a medieval feast.Roast pig: Whole roast pig was a showpiece at grand medieval banquets, often brought in with an apple in its mouth.
Things at a medieval feast.Goblet: Goblets of metal or glass were status symbols, and nobles' feasts often used them while commoners drank from wood or horn.
Things at a medieval feast.Jester: Court jesters had license to mock even the king, and some, like Will Sommers under Henry VIII, were beloved friends of the throne.
Things at a medieval feast.Minstrel: Minstrels were wandering musicians who carried songs and news between castles, acting as living newspapers.
Things at a medieval feast.Mead: Mead, fermented honey and water, is among the oldest alcoholic drinks, and was the favored drink of Norse and Anglo-Saxon halls.
Things at a medieval feast.Lute: The lute reached Europe from the Arab oud, and its name likely comes from the Arabic al-ud.
Things at a medieval feast.Candles: Candles of beeswax were a luxury, and most people made do with smoky tallow ones from animal fat.
Things at a medieval feast.Banquet table: Great halls used long boards on trestles, and 'board and lodging' and 'chairman' trace their roots to such tables.
Things at a medieval feast.King: A king at the high table sat above the salt: a large salt cellar marked rank, so lesser guests sat 'below the salt'.
Things at a medieval feast.Bread loaves: Bread served as plates: stale 'trenchers' soaked up gravy and were then eaten or given to the poor.
Things at a medieval feast.Roast boar: Boar was a prized dish, and hunting wild boar was a noble sport, often served with a ceremonial apple in its jaws.
Things at a medieval feast.Pizza delivery: Pizza as we know it came from Naples in the 1700s and 1800s, and delivery is far newer, so no medieval feast had either.
Things at a medieval feast.Soda can: Aluminum cans date from the 1950s, centuries too late, and soft drinks as we know them came from the 1800s.
Things at a medieval feast.Ketchup bottle: Ketchup began as a Chinese fish sauce, and tomato versions came only in the 1800s; tomatoes reached Europe after 1492.
Things at a medieval feast.Microwave: Microwave ovens came from the 1940s, when a radar engineer found a candy bar had melted in his pocket.
Things at a medieval feast.Plastic fork: Forks were rare in medieval Europe, and diners ate with knives and fingers; plastic wasn't invented until the 1800s.
Things at a medieval feast.Hot dog: Hot dogs arrived with German immigrants in the US, and frankfurters took their name from Frankfurt, in the 1800s.
Things at a medieval feast.Fortune cookie: Fortune cookies are a Californian invention of the early 1900s, not Chinese, so no medieval feast had one.
Things at a medieval feast.Popcorn: Popcorn is native to the Americas, which medieval Europeans didn't know existed, so it is a New World snack.
Things at a medieval feast.Potato chips: Potato chips were reportedly made in 1853 in Saratoga Springs, New York, and potatoes only reached Europe in the 1500s.
Things at a medieval feast.Disco ball: Disco balls are 1970s, though mirrored globes existed in the 1920s dance halls; a medieval hall had torchlight instead.
Things at a medieval feast.Credit card: Credit cards arrived in the 1950s, and a medieval host would have paid in coin or in kind.
Things at a medieval feast.Chocolate cake: Chocolate came to Europe from the Aztec world in the 1500s, and chocolate cake appeared much later.
Things at a medieval feast.Paper napkins: Paper napkins arrived in the 1800s, and medieval diners wiped their hands on a shared cloth or the tablecloth.

British Army ranks.Private: The lowest rank, but many regiments swap the title for their own, such as Guardsman, Trooper or Gunner.
British Army ranks.Lance Corporal: The first promotion, marked by one chevron; the word lance comes from an old term for a temporary acting rank.
British Army ranks.Corporal: Two chevrons; the word comes from the Italian for head, since a corporal leads a small group.
British Army ranks.Sergeant: Three chevrons; the word comes from Latin serviens, meaning servant, and once described a household attendant.
British Army ranks.Staff Sergeant: Shown by a crown above three chevrons, it ranks above Sergeant and often marks a senior role in running a unit.
British Army ranks.Lieutenant: Said 'leftenant' in Britain; it comes from French for place-holding, someone who stands in for a superior.
British Army ranks.Captain: Worn as three pips on the shoulder; the word traces back to the Latin caput, head.
British Army ranks.Major: Wears a crown on the shoulder and often commands a company of around a hundred soldiers.
British Army ranks.Colonel: Spelled one way, said 'kernel': English took an Italian spelling but kept the older French-Spanish pronunciation with an r.
British Army ranks.Brigadier: Commands a brigade of several thousand; it ranks above Colonel but is not formally a general in the British Army.
British Army ranks.Field Marshal: Crossed batons mark the army's highest rank, now rarely awarded and mostly held as an honor.
British Army ranks.General: Sits just below Field Marshal and is held by only a handful of the army's top commanders.
British Army ranks.Admiral: A naval rank, not army: the word comes from Arabic amir, meaning commander.
British Army ranks.Petty Officer: A naval non-commissioned officer; petty comes from French petit, meaning small.
British Army ranks.Commodore: A navy rank between captain and rear admiral, also given to senior captains of merchant fleets.
British Army ranks.Rear Admiral: A naval rank named from the old fleet division where this admiral commanded the rear squadron.
British Army ranks.Midshipman: A naval trainee officer whose name is said to come from serving amidships.
British Army ranks.Air Marshal: An RAF rank, equal to an army Lieutenant General, so a trap for anyone expecting a ground-force title.
British Army ranks.Wing Commander: An RAF rank, equal to an army Lieutenant Colonel, named for commanding a flying wing.
British Army ranks.Squadron Leader: An RAF rank equal to Major; Douglas Bader led a fighter squadron under this title in 1940.
British Army ranks.Flight Lieutenant: An RAF rank equal to Captain; the RAF took naval-style titles when it formed in 1918.
British Army ranks.Group Captain: An RAF rank equal to Colonel, one step below Air Commodore.
British Army ranks.Leading Seaman: A junior naval rating, comparable to an army Lance Corporal, so it belongs to the navy.
British Army ranks.Pilot Officer: The lowest RAF commissioned rank, equal to an army Second Lieutenant.

Things an archaeologist uses.Trowel: Many archaeologists keep the same pointed trowel for decades, and a worn one is a badge of experience.
Things an archaeologist uses.Brush: Soft brushes reveal fragile bone and pottery without scratching.
Things an archaeologist uses.Sieve: Excavated soil is screened through mesh to catch tiny beads, seeds, bones and coins that eyes miss.
Things an archaeologist uses.Shovel: Excavators use shovels to remove loose topsoil, but near finds they switch to trowels.
Things an archaeologist uses.Measuring tape: Everything is measured in three dimensions, because where a find lies matters as much as what it is.
Things an archaeologist uses.Grid string: Strings divide a site into squares, as in the grid system promoted by Mortimer Wheeler, so each find can be located exactly.
Things an archaeologist uses.Camera: Digging destroys the layers it reveals, so photographs are the permanent record.
Things an archaeologist uses.Notebook: Because excavation cannot be undone, field notes and drawings are what remains of the dig.
Things an archaeologist uses.Bucket: Each bucket of soil is labeled by layer, so any find can be traced back to where it lay.
Things an archaeologist uses.Dental pick: Dentists' picks clear soil around fragile bone and teeth, and archaeologists borrowed them.
Things an archaeologist uses.Finds bag: Small bags are tagged with site, layer and date, because context is what makes an artifact tell its story.
Things an archaeologist uses.Telescope: Astronomers use it, and archaeoastronomers study how ancient sites align with the stars, usually with maps and software.
Things an archaeologist uses.Stethoscope: Doctors use it, though archaeologists do put mummies through medical CT scans.
Things an archaeologist uses.Lasso: Indiana Jones used a whip, and no real archaeologist uses a lasso.
Things an archaeologist uses.Harpoon: Whalers use it, though archaeologists sometimes dig up ancient harpoon points.
Things an archaeologist uses.Gavel: A mallet for judges, not for digging up the past.
Things an archaeologist uses.Easel: An artist's stand, as far from a trench as it gets.
Things an archaeologist uses.Whisk: A kitchen tool that mixes batter, while a soft brush does the delicate work at a dig.
Things an archaeologist uses.Defibrillator: It delivers a shock to restart hearts, and the first human defibrillation took place in 1947.
Things an archaeologist uses.Cash register: James Ritty invented it in 1879 in Ohio to stop employee theft.
Things an archaeologist uses.Fishing rod: An angler's tool, though fishing gear is a common archaeological find.
Things an archaeologist uses.Rolling pin: A baker's tool for flattening dough, not for flattening soil.
Things an archaeologist uses.Sewing machine: Isaac Singer's improved machine of 1851 made sewing fast and common.
Things an archaeologist uses.Saddle: Archaeologists study ancient saddles, and stirrups appear in China around the 4th century.

Animals that have had real jobs.Dog: Dogs were domesticated thousands of years ago, and their jobs range from herding to bomb detection, making them the most varied working animal.
Animals that have had real jobs.Horse: Engine power is still measured in horsepower, a unit James Watt invented to sell steam engines to horse-using customers.
Animals that have had real jobs.Pigeon: Pigeons carried messages in wars, and Cher Ami, a World War I pigeon, delivered word that helped save a trapped US battalion.
Animals that have had real jobs.Elephant: Elephants have hauled timber and carried people for centuries, especially in Asia's logging trade, and armies once used them in battle.
Animals that have had real jobs.Ox: Oxen pulled ploughs and carts for thousands of years, and an ox is a trained adult of cattle, usually male and castrated.
Animals that have had real jobs.Camel: Camels carried caravans along the Silk Road, and a thirsty dromedary can drink over 100 litres in a few minutes.
Animals that have had real jobs.Ferret: Ferrets were bred to hunt rabbits by slipping down burrows, and have also been used to pull cables through narrow pipes.
Animals that have had real jobs.Falcon: Falconry is thousands of years old, and falcons are still used at airports to scare birds away from runways.
Animals that have had real jobs.Donkey: Donkeys have carried goods and people across rough, dry country for millennia and still work in Africa, Asia and Latin America.
Animals that have had real jobs.Canary: Coal miners carried canaries to detect carbon monoxide, since the birds showed distress first; Britain ended the practice in 1986.
Animals that have had real jobs.Pig: Pigs traditionally hunted truffles thanks to their strong noses, but they tend to eat the prize, so dogs took over.
Animals that have had real jobs.Dolphin: The US Navy trains dolphins to locate underwater mines using their natural sonar.
Animals that have had real jobs.Mule: A mule is the offspring of a male donkey and a female horse; it's usually sterile, yet strong and sure-footed.
Animals that have had real jobs.Sea lion: The US Navy has trained sea lions to find lost equipment and detect swimmers in harbours, using their sharp underwater vision.
Animals that have had real jobs.Sloth: Sloths move so slowly that algae grows in their fur, and they spend most of the day hanging or asleep, so nobody employs them.
Animals that have had real jobs.Koala: Koalas sleep around 18 to 22 hours a day on a low-energy eucalyptus diet, leaving little room for a job.
Animals that have had real jobs.Jellyfish: Jellyfish have no brain or heart, so training one is impossible, though a glowing protein from one species won a Nobel Prize.
Animals that have had real jobs.Platypus: The platypus is venomous and senses electric fields, but it's shy and hard to keep, and has never been given a job.
Animals that have had real jobs.Starfish: Starfish have no brain and move slowly on tube feet, so humans haven't managed to make workers of them.
Animals that have had real jobs.Flamingo: Flamingos get their pink colour from carotenoid pigments in their food, and while they're stars of zoos, they don't work.
Animals that have had real jobs.Snail: Snails are farmed for food, but none has ever held a job; a snail can sleep for years during dry spells.
Animals that have had real jobs.Sea cucumber: Sea cucumbers are harvested for food, not as workers; they filter the seabed, which helps recycle nutrients.
Animals that have had real jobs.Hedgehog: Hedgehogs eat slugs and beetles, a handy garden service, but nobody has ever trained one for a real job.
Animals that have had real jobs.Panda: Pandas spend around 12 hours a day eating bamboo, and while they serve as China's diplomatic ambassadors, they're not workers.

Things you'd see in a boardroom.Long table: Boardroom tables are often big oval or rectangular slabs, designed so every director can see everyone else.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Projector: The first digital projectors reached offices in the 1990s, replacing overhead projectors that used transparencies.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Whiteboard: Whiteboards took over from chalkboards in many offices because dry-erase markers leave no dust.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Conference phone: A star-shaped conference speakerphone lets remote directors join the meeting, with microphones aimed in every direction.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Leather chairs: Leather chairs signal status, and high-backed ones are the classic executive seat, often reserved for the head of the table.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Water jugs: Water jugs and glasses stand on boardroom tables so long meetings don't leave directors parched.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Presentation screen: Wall screens in meeting rooms have replaced pull-down projection screens, and many double as video call displays.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Agenda: The word agenda comes from Latin for 'things to be done', and a good one keeps a meeting on track.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Flip chart: Flip charts are large pads on an easel, still popular because they need no power and the pages can be taped to a wall.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Laser pointer: Presentation laser pointers are usually under 5 milliwatts, safe for a quick flash but never to be aimed at eyes.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Bunk beds: Bunk beds suit dorms and barracks; a board never sleeps in the meeting room, or it's a very long meeting.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Hay bale: Hay bales are farm fodder, though some trendy offices use them as rustic seating; board directors prefer leather.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Hot tub: A hot tub is for relaxing, which is not what happens in a tense board meeting.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Trampoline: Trampolines bounce; board decisions, hopefully, don't, so they belong in back gardens and gyms.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Ball pit: Some tech startups install ball pits for fun, but the stuffy boardroom is the opposite of play.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Dental chair: A dental chair reclines and has a lamp above, and in a boardroom it would suggest the meeting is about drilling.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Fire pole: A fire pole lets firefighters slide quickly between floors; some playful offices install slides, but not boardrooms.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Pulpit: A pulpit is an elevated lectern in churches for sermons, so it wouldn't be found in a business meeting room.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Slot machine: A slot machine is for casinos, whereas a boardroom is for the opposite kind of gamble: carefully weighed decisions.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Treadmill: Treadmills belong in gyms, though walking meetings on treadmill desks have been tried in some offices.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Pottery wheel: A pottery wheel spins clay into bowls and vases, a craft for artists' studios, not for directors.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Jukebox: A jukebox plays music for coins and was big in 1950s diners, not in business meetings.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Kiddie pool: A kiddie pool is a shallow inflatable pool for toddlers, whereas boardrooms have water jugs for sipping.
Things you'd see in a boardroom.Barber's chair: Barber's chairs pump up and down for cutting hair, whereas boardroom chairs stay put on wheels.

Things you'd find in a warehouse.Pallets: A standard North American pallet is 48 by 40 inches, and shipping systems worldwide are built around pallet sizes.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Forklift: A heavy counterweight at the rear keeps a forklift from tipping when it lifts a load, and drivers need training.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Shelving racks: Warehouse racking is built so forklifts can slot pallets straight in, and some stand dozens of metres tall.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Loading dock: Dock levelers bridge the gap between a truck bed and the floor so forklifts can roll straight in.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Barcode scanner: The first product scanned at a checkout was a pack of Wrigley's gum in Ohio in 1974.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Shrink wrap: Heat-shrink film tightens around goods when warmed; the stretch wrap on pallets is a different, cling kind.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Pallet jack: A hand-pumped hydraulic jack lets one person move a loaded pallet weighing over a tonne.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Cardboard boxes: Corrugated boxes took off in the late 1800s; the wavy inner layer gives them their rigidity.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Conveyor belt: Henry Ford's Highland Park plant adopted a moving assembly line in 1913, slashing Model T build times.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Inventory: The word comes from Latin for a list of things found, and warehouses spend lots of effort counting it.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Altar: A place of worship; the Latin altare relates to a high place, and you won't find one among the pallets.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Dental chair: The hydraulic dental chair was patented by Basil Wilkerson in the 1870s, but no warehouse stores one.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Jury box: A courtroom seating area; in many English-speaking trials twelve jurors sit there, with no storage involved.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Hot tub: Candido Jacuzzi developed his whirlpool bath in the 1950s to ease his son's arthritis.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Chandelier: A hanging light with branches; the word comes from French chandelle, a candle.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Pulpit: The raised stand in a church for preachers; the name derives from Latin pulpitum, meaning platform.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Ball pit: A pool of lightweight plastic balls for children's play centres, not a storage space, though it holds thousands.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Operating table: We still say 'operating theatre' because surgery was once performed before an audience.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Grand piano: A concert grand has about 230 strings, together pulling with roughly 20 tonnes of tension.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Bunk beds: Stacked sleeping berths were common on ships and trains long before they moved into children's rooms.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Jukebox: The first coin-operated music machine appeared in a San Francisco saloon in 1889, playing wax cylinders.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Barber's chair: Barber poles are red and white because barbers once also performed bloodletting, and the chair is a salon item.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Hymn books: Churches provide them; the Bay Psalm Book of 1640 was the first book printed in the English colonies.
Things you'd find in a warehouse.Fireplace: Latin focus meant hearth, so the word 'focus' itself began at the fireside, not the warehouse.

Famous streets and roads.Abbey Road: The Beatles walked across the zebra crossing here for their 1969 album cover, and the crossing is now a protected landmark.
Famous streets and roads.Broadway: Broadway runs the length of Manhattan, following an old Native American trail, and gives its name to the theatre district.
Famous streets and roads.Champs-Élysées: The Champs-Élysées is where the Tour de France traditionally finishes, in front of the Arc de Triomphe.
Famous streets and roads.Fifth Avenue: Fifth Avenue is the dividing line between east and west addresses on Manhattan's streets.
Famous streets and roads.Wall Street: Wall Street was named after a wall built by Dutch settlers in the 1600s, and it's now a nickname for America's financial markets.
Famous streets and roads.Lombard Street: This San Francisco block, famously crooked, has eight hairpin turns and is often called the crookedest street in the world.
Famous streets and roads.Oxford Street: Oxford Street, in London, is Europe's busiest shopping street and has over 300 shops along about 1.5 miles.
Famous streets and roads.Downing Street: Number 10 has been the British prime minister's home since the 1730s, and Robert Walpole was the first to live there.
Famous streets and roads.Hollywood Boulevard: The Hollywood Walk of Fame, with more than 2,600 stars set into the pavement, runs along this boulevard.
Famous streets and roads.Bourbon Street: Bourbon Street in New Orleans is named after the French royal house, not the whiskey.
Famous streets and roads.Las Ramblas: La Rambla in Barcelona is a tree-lined pedestrian boulevard; "rambla" comes from the Arabic for a dry riverbed.
Famous streets and roads.Rodeo Drive: Rodeo Drive, in Beverly Hills, is a luxury shopping street, pronounced "ro-DAY-oh", not like the cowboy event.
Famous streets and roads.Baker Street: Sherlock Holmes's address at 221B Baker Street didn't exist when Conan Doyle wrote the stories.
Famous streets and roads.Times Square: Times Square is a junction rather than a street, named after the New York Times, which moved there in 1904.
Famous streets and roads.Hyde Park: Hyde Park is a London park, famous for Speakers' Corner, where anyone can make a speech.
Famous streets and roads.Central Park: Central Park is a park, not a street, though roads wind through it; it covers about 843 acres of Manhattan.
Famous streets and roads.Red Square: Red Square in Moscow is a square, and its name originally meant "beautiful", not the colour.
Famous streets and roads.Trafalgar Square: Trafalgar Square in London is a public square with Nelson's Column at its centre, not a street; it commemorates a naval victory in 1805.
Famous streets and roads.Thames: The Thames is a river, and at roughly 215 miles it is the longest river entirely in England.
Famous streets and roads.Seine: The Seine is the river flowing through Paris, and the name is on the streets that line its banks, but it's a waterway.
Famous streets and roads.Hudson: The Hudson is a river that flows past New York; Henry Hudson explored it in 1609.
Famous streets and roads.Plaza Mayor: Plaza Mayor in Madrid is a large public square, once the site of bullfights and royal celebrations.
Famous streets and roads.St Mark's Square: St Mark's Square in Venice is a famous piazza, frequently flooded in high tides and home to hundreds of pigeons.
Famous streets and roads.Champ de Mars: The Champ de Mars is a park beneath the Eiffel Tower, named for a Roman parade ground, and not a road.

Things in an Old West town.Saloon: Western saloons served whiskey and card games, and the 'swinging doors' were often half-height 'batwing' doors.
Things in an Old West town.Sheriff's office: The sheriff, from the English 'shire reeve', often had a jail and a gun rack in the same building.
Things in an Old West town.Jail: Many Old West jails were small, one-room buildings with only a few cells.
Things in an Old West town.Livery stable: A livery stable boarded and rented horses, much like a modern car rental and garage combined.
Things in an Old West town.General store: The general store sold everything from flour to nails, and was often the center of town life.
Things in an Old West town.Hitching post: Riders tied horses to hitching posts outside saloons, a Western prop in many films.
Things in an Old West town.Swinging doors: The short batwing doors let air in while keeping horses from peering in, and gave the cowboy dramatic entrances.
Things in an Old West town.Stagecoach: Stagecoaches like Wells Fargo's carried passengers and mail, and a trip from Missouri to California took about 25 days.
Things in an Old West town.Tumbleweed: Tumbleweeds are dried plants that roll to scatter seeds, and the famous Western kind, the Russian thistle, came from Eurasia.
Things in an Old West town.Blacksmith: The blacksmith shod horses and mended wagon wheels, and so was one of the town's most essential workers.
Things in an Old West town.Bank: Frontier banks were prime targets for outlaws, and some, like Jesse James's gang, struck again and again.
Things in an Old West town.Parking meter: Parking meters were invented in 1935 in Oklahoma City, long after the Wild West era ended.
Things in an Old West town.Traffic light: The first electric traffic light was installed in Cleveland in 1914, after the Old West was gone.
Things in an Old West town.Skyscraper: The first skyscraper, the Home Insurance Building in Chicago, rose in 1885, when the frontier was nearly closed.
Things in an Old West town.Gas station: Gas stations came with automobiles, and the first drive-in filling station opened in Pittsburgh in 1913.
Things in an Old West town.Escalator: The first escalator was installed at Coney Island in 1896, and Old West towns had no use for one.
Things in an Old West town.Subway: The first US subway opened in Boston in 1897, a city rather than frontier technology.
Things in an Old West town.Neon sign: Neon signs arrived in the 1910s in France, and don't fit frontier towns' oil lamps.
Things in an Old West town.Vending machine: The earliest vending machine, in Roman Egypt, dispensed holy water, but the coin-operated type came later.
Things in an Old West town.Supermarket: The first supermarket, Piggly Wiggly, opened in Memphis in 1916, after the Old West era.
Things in an Old West town.Cinema: Movies began in the 1890s, near the end of the Old West, so it's an odd fit for a saloon town.
Things in an Old West town.Car wash: The first automatic car wash opened in Detroit in 1914, and the Old West had been gone for a generation.
Things in an Old West town.Drive-thru: Drive-thrus rose with car culture and fast food in the 1940s and 1950s, long after cowboys.
Things in an Old West town.Helipad: Helicopters and their pads arrived in the 1940s, decades after the frontier.

Diwali traditions (not Holi).Diya: Small clay oil lamps lit to celebrate light over darkness; Ayodhya has set world records by lighting over a million of them.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Rangoli: Colorful floor patterns made at entrances with powder or flower petals to welcome the goddess.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Goddess Lakshmi: The goddess of wealth, invited into clean, lit homes; many families begin the main night with prayers to her.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Ladoo: Round sweets of gram flour or semolina and ghee, a classic Diwali gift between neighbors.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Kaju katli: A diamond-shaped fudge of cashew paste, often topped with edible silver leaf.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Dhanteras: The festival's first day, two days before the main night, when people buy gold, silver or utensils for luck.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Mithai: The general word for Indian sweets, boxes of which are exchanged among friends and neighbors during Diwali.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Oil lamps: They symbolize the victory of light over darkness, and many families keep them burning all night.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Firecrackers: So central that air pollution in Indian cities often spikes after Diwali, prompting restrictions in some.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Sparklers: Children's favorites, called phooljhari or 'flower showers', give a safer way to join the fireworks.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Ganesha: The elephant-headed god of beginnings, worshipped beside Lakshmi on Diwali night.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Rama's return: Many Hindus celebrate Rama's return to Ayodhya after 14 years in exile, when villagers lit lamps to guide him home.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Gulal: Bright powder flung at Holi, the spring festival of colors, not at Diwali, the autumn festival of lights.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Pichkari: A water gun used to squirt colored water at Holi.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Thandai: A cold, spiced milk drink strongly linked to Holi celebrations.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Gujiya: Sweet fried dumplings with a milk-solid filling, most associated with Holi.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Holika Dahan: The bonfire lit the night before Holi, recalling the story of Prahlad and Holika.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Colored powder: Thrown at Holi in spring; Diwali is about lights, not color fights.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Water balloons: A Holi staple, tossed by the thousands in the spring color festival; Diwali is about lamps and sweets instead.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Bhang: A cannabis-leaf drink traditionally served at Holi.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Phagwah: The Holi name used by Indo-Caribbean communities in places like Guyana and Trinidad.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Dol Jatra: A spring festival in Bengal where an image of Krishna is swung and colors are thrown, a cousin of Holi.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Lathmar Holi: In Barsana, women playfully beat men with sticks during this Holi tradition.
Diwali traditions (not Holi).Spring bonfire: Holi's Holika bonfire marks the arrival of spring, while Diwali falls in autumn.

Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Bonjour: French 'good day', used until evening; in France, walking into a shop without saying it is considered rude.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Hola: Spanish hello with a silent H, so it sounds like 'ola'; the word was once also a sailors' call, like 'ahoy'.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Hallo: German and Dutch hello, a close cousin of English 'hello', which spread widely with the invention of the telephone.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Namaste: Sanskrit for 'I bow to you', said with palms pressed together across India and Nepal, for both greeting and parting.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Konnichiwa: A Japanese greeting that grew from a phrase meaning 'as for today...', used from late morning through the afternoon.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Ni hao: Chinese for literally 'you good'; many speakers use it mostly with strangers, not friends or family.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Guten Tag: German 'good day', more formal than 'hallo'; in southern Germany people often say 'Gruess Gott' instead.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Buongiorno: Italian 'good day'; later in the afternoon Italians switch to 'buonasera', so timing matters.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Jambo: A Swahili hello widely used with tourists in East Africa, while locals often say 'hujambo' to one person.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Sawubona: Zulu for 'I see you', answered with 'Yebo, sikhona', meaning 'yes, we are here'.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Merhaba: A Turkish hello borrowed from the Arabic 'marhaba', which spread across the Ottoman world.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Kia ora: A Maori greeting that literally wishes life and health, and now standard in New Zealand English too.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.G'day: Short for 'good day', the classic Australian hello, often followed by 'mate'.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Au revoir: Means 'until we see each other again' in French, so a goodbye and not a hello.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Adios: From the old phrase 'a Dios', meaning 'to God': a Spanish goodbye, not a greeting.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Sayonara: A Japanese goodbye with a sense of finality; most people use other phrases for casual partings.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Auf Wiedersehen: German 'until seeing again', a goodbye that is traditionally polite and a bit formal.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Arrivederci: Italian 'until we see each other again', a goodbye famous from song and film.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Tschuss: A casual German goodbye, a distant cousin of 'adieu' by way of Low German, and not a hello.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Gracias: Spanish for 'thank you', from the Latin word for grace, so it is thanks rather than a greeting.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Merci: French for 'thank you', from the Latin for 'wages' or 'favor', so it is thanks, not hello.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Danke: German for 'thank you', related to the English word 'think', so it is thanks, not a greeting.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Arigato: Japanese thanks, with a root that means 'rare' or 'difficult to come by', so it is no greeting.
Ways to say hello (not goodbye or thanks.Spasibo: Russian thanks, believed to come from 'spasi Bog', meaning 'God save you', so a thank-you rather than a hello.
